lessons.objective: Explain why Moses connects courage with God’s presence.
lessons.context: Moses is preparing Israel for life under Joshua’s leadership. Being strong does not mean pretending the transition is easy. The reason for courage is the LORD’s faithfulness, rather than a guarantee that every encounter will be painless.
lessons.takeaway: Before one difficult conversation, pause and remember that courage can include asking for help.

questions.prompt: What reason does Moses give Israel for courage?

options.text: The LORD goes with them and will not forsake them.
They already know how every challenge will end.
Strong people never experience fear.
Joshua will remove the need to trust God.

questions.explanation: The verse grounds courage in God going with his people. It does not say they already know the outcome or cannot feel fear.

questions.prompt: Which response fits this lesson when a hard conversation approaches?

options.text: Acknowledge the fear and take a thoughtful step with trust in God.
Wait until every trace of fear disappears.
Assume God’s presence guarantees agreement.
Hide the difficulty so that needing help stays secret.

questions.explanation: Courage can coexist with fear. Pausing, seeking support, and acting wisely fit the teaching without claiming a certain outcome.

lessons.objective: Recognize God’s help as the basis for strength in Isaiah 41:10.
lessons.context: Isaiah addresses God’s people as those whom God has chosen and will not abandon. The repeated “I will” directs attention to God’s action. Strength here is received from God; it is not a test of whether someone can make herself feel capable.
lessons.takeaway: Ask someone trustworthy for help with one task, and bring that need to God in prayer.

questions.prompt: Where does the support described in this verse come from?

options.text: God promises to strengthen, help, and uphold his people.
People must prove their independence before God helps.
Feeling confident is the condition for receiving help.
The verse asks people to ignore their limitations.

questions.explanation: God is the subject of the promises to strengthen, help, and uphold. The lesson does not make self-sufficiency a condition of care.

questions.prompt: What is a fitting response when your energy runs low?

options.text: Name your need and ask for appropriate support.
Conceal weakness so that God can see your strength.
Treat exhaustion as proof that God has abandoned you.
Take on more tasks to earn God’s help.

questions.explanation: Asking for support acknowledges a real need. It follows the lesson’s invitation to receive help without disguising weakness.

lessons.objective: Describe what it means to call God a present refuge in trouble.
lessons.context: A refuge provides shelter while danger is real. Psalm 46 continues with images of a shaking earth and roaring waters. Its confidence does not depend on a stable world: God’s nearness is the reason the community can turn to him in upheaval.
lessons.takeaway: Before replying to a stressful message, take a short pause for prayer and choose a measured response.

questions.prompt: What does “a very present help in trouble” emphasize?

options.text: God can be turned to while the trouble is happening.
Prayer only becomes appropriate after the problem is solved.
Faithful people never encounter instability.
A refuge removes every practical responsibility.

questions.explanation: The psalm names God as help in trouble, not merely afterward. Refuge describes support amid instability.

questions.prompt: Which action applies the lesson to a stressful message?

options.text: Pause for prayer, then respond with care even if the problem remains.
Assume that prayer means no reply will ever be needed.
Wait to approach God until you have solved the problem.
Treat feeling stressed as a failure of faith.

questions.explanation: A pause for prayer makes room for dependence and a thoughtful response. The lesson does not promise an instant resolution.

lessons.objective: Distinguish God’s commitment from a promise of a life without opposition.
lessons.context: Romans 8 speaks of suffering as well as hope. Paul’s question points to God’s saving commitment, expressed in Christ, as the decisive ground for confidence. Opposition remains real; it does not have the final authority to separate believers from God’s love.
lessons.takeaway: Consider whether a criticism contains useful truth; receive what helps and avoid letting the comment define your worth.

questions.prompt: What is Paul emphasizing when he asks, “If God is for us, who can be against us?”

options.text: God’s saving commitment is greater than the opposition believers face.
Believers will never encounter anyone who disagrees with them.
Every personal decision receives God’s approval.
Winning arguments proves a person belongs to God.

questions.explanation: In context, Paul grounds confidence in God’s saving work. He does not deny suffering or promise universal approval.

questions.prompt: How can this teaching guide a response to criticism?

options.text: Consider useful correction without making the comment your final verdict.
Dismiss all correction because no critic can ever be right.
Win every argument before allowing yourself to rest.
Assume a painful comment means God has stopped caring.

questions.explanation: God’s love offers a stable basis for worth while leaving room for honest correction. Confidence does not require winning every argument.

lessons.objective: Read Jeremiah’s promise of hope in the setting of a long exile.
lessons.context: Jeremiah’s letter tells exiles to build homes and seek the welfare of the city where they live. Restoration lies beyond a long wait. The promise addresses a community’s future under God’s care; it is not a timetable for individual success or an assurance of wealth.
lessons.takeaway: Choose one useful action within today’s limits while allowing yourself to be honest about the waiting.

options.text: A community in exile faces a long wait for restoration.
A traveler is guaranteed immediate success in a new business.
A community has already escaped every hardship.
Jeremiah promises that each personal plan will succeed.

questions.explanation: The promise belongs to Jeremiah’s letter to the exiles. The surrounding instruction anticipates patient life in exile, rather than immediate escape.

questions.prompt: Which response best fits this lesson during a slow season?

options.text: Take one faithful, useful step without demanding an immediate outcome.
Treat waiting as proof that life has lost all meaning.
Read the promise as a guarantee of quick financial gain.
Stop contributing until the entire future is clear.

questions.explanation: Patient hope can support useful action today. It does not require a promised deadline or a particular personal outcome.
